lead: A service level agreement (SLA) is the written promise a cloud provider makes to a customer. A service level objective (SLO) is the stricter target the provider or team aims for inside that promise. A service level indicator (SLI) is the number actually measured, such as uptime or latency. The gap between SLO and SLA is the warning space: before contract credits are due, the team sees the error budget run out and slows risky releases. This chapter shows how the three fit together, how nines become minutes, and how series services multiply their promises.
prereq: You need: availability and replication in Chapter 2.5 and service models in Unit 1.

sections.h3: SLI, SLO and SLA are three different things

blocks.text: A service level indicator (SLI) is the number a system measures. For uptime, the SLI is uptime minutes ÷ total minutes in the window. For an API, it may be successful requests ÷ valid requests. The window is part of the definition: 99.95% over one month is not the same as 99.95% over one day.

A service level objective (SLO) is the target for that SLI. Example: 99.95% of valid API requests succeed in a 30-day window, checked by one-minute probes. An SLO is internal. It guides releases and alerts.

A service level agreement (SLA) is the contract. It names the parties, the service, the metric, the measurement window, exclusions, support, and the credits or penalties if the promise is missed. The SLA is what a customer can claim against; the SLO is the stricter operating target that leaves room before that claim.

A good SLA is measurable by both sides. 'Fast support' is not an SLA. '95% of severity-1 tickets get a human response within 30 minutes, measured monthly' is testable. Exclusions usually cover scheduled maintenance, customer misconfiguration and force majeure.

sections.h3: Nines, allowed downtime and error budgets

blocks.text: Availability is written as a fraction A or a percentage. 99.9% is A = 0.999. The missing fraction 1 − A is the allowed unavailability. Each extra nine makes the allowed failure ten times smaller: 99% is two nines, 99.9% is three nines.

blocks.where: D is the allowed downtime in minutes; T is the measurement window in minutes; A is the promised availability as a fraction, so 99.9% is A = 0.999.

blocks.text: For a repairable service, A = MTBF ÷ (MTBF + MTTR), where MTBF is mean time between failures and MTTR is mean time to repair. Cloud SLAs usually measure with probes, not MTBF, but the arithmetic of allowed downtime is the same.

blocks.where: Budget is the allowed failure time in minutes; T is the window in minutes; SLO is the objective as a fraction, so 99.95% is 0.9995.

blocks.text: The error budget is the allowed failure inside the SLO. If the SLO is 99.95%, the budget is 0.05% of the window. When the budget is spent, the team freezes risky changes or adds reliability work. If the SLO is looser than the SLA, the budget is larger than the contract allows, so it gives no early warning before credits are due.

blocks.where: A<sub>total</sub> is the availability of the whole chain; A<sub>1</sub> to A<sub>n</sub> are the availabilities of services in series, each as a fraction.

blocks.text: For services in series, a request must pass every part, so availabilities multiply. Two 99.9% parts give 0.999 × 0.999 = 0.998001, about 99.8%, not 99.9%. Parallel replicas with failover work differently; see Chapter 2.5. Composite SLA is the product, not the minimum.

Two recovery numbers appear in many SLAs. Recovery time objective (RTO) is the maximum acceptable time to restore service after a failure. Recovery point objective (RPO) is the maximum acceptable data loss, measured in time. RTO 15 minutes and RPO 5 minutes means the service must be back within 15 minutes and may lose at most the last 5 minutes of data. RTO is about downtime; RPO is about data.

Monitoring makes the SLA auditable. Synthetic probes call the service every minute from outside; real-user monitoring records actual request success and latency; logs and incident records explain gaps. The monthly report should show the SLI, the SLO status, the error budget spent, incidents and any excluded time.

Credits are not automatic in most contracts. The customer usually files a claim inside a stated period, and the provider checks the measurement and exclusions. See Unit 4 for billing and cost models and Unit 6 for security clauses and audits. Do not quote one provider's percentage as a universal rule.

examples.question: A 30-day month has 30 × 24 × 60 = 43,200 minutes. A service has an SLA of 99.9% monthly availability and an SLO of 99.95% monthly availability. Actual downtime in the month is 30 minutes. (a) Find the allowed downtime under the SLA and under the SLO. (b) State whether the SLA and SLO are met and whether service credits are due. (c) A request passes two services in series with availabilities 99.9% and 99.95%. Find the composite availability and its allowed downtime in the same month.
steps: Actual downtime is 30.0 minutes. 30.0 ≤ 43.2, so the SLA is met. 30.0 > 21.6, so the SLO is breached. The error budget is spent, so freeze risky releases. No credits are due because the SLA is met.
examples.answer: The SLA allows 43.2 minutes and is met; the SLO allows 21.6 minutes and is breached; no credits are due; the two-service series has availability 0.9985005 (99.85005%) and allows 64.7784 minutes (about 64.8 minutes) of downtime.
examples.check:
T = 30 * 24 * 60
sla_allowed = T * (1 - 0.999)
slo_allowed = T * (1 - 0.9995)
actual = 30.0
composite = 0.999 * 0.9995
allowed = T * (1 - composite)
print(f"{sla_allowed:.1f}")
print(f"{slo_allowed:.1f}")
print(f"{actual:.1f}")
print(f"{composite:.7f}")
print(f"{composite * 100:.5f}")
print(f"{allowed:.4f}")
print(f"{allowed:.1f}")

traps: An SLO must be stricter than the SLA. If it is looser, the error budget is larger than the contract allows and gives no warning before credits are due.
Composite availability for services in series is the product, not the minimum. Two 99.9% services in series give about 99.8%, not 99.9%.
A percentage is not a fraction. 99.9% means A = 0.999, and allowed downtime is T × (1 − A), not T × A.
SLA credits are usually not automatic. The customer must claim inside a stated period, and exclusions such as scheduled maintenance or customer misconfiguration may remove the breach.
RTO and RPO are different promises. RTO limits how long the service may stay down; RPO limits how much recent data may be lost.

quiz.q: Define SLI, SLO and SLA in one line each.
quiz.a: SLI: the measured value, such as uptime ÷ window. SLO: the internal target for that SLI. SLA: the contract with the customer, with credits or penalties.

quiz.q: Why should the SLO be stricter than the SLA?
quiz.a: The gap gives warning. The error budget runs out before credits are due, so the team can freeze releases and fix reliability without breaking the contract.

quiz.q: A 30-day month has 43,200 minutes. An SLA promises 99.95% availability. What downtime does it allow?
Two services in series have 99.9% and 99.9% availability. A manager says the pair gives 99.9%. Correct the claim.
quiz.a: Both must work, so multiply: 0.999 × 0.999 = 0.998001, about 99.8%. The minimum is wrong for a series chain.

quiz.q: List four parts of an SLA.
quiz.a: Parties, service description, metric and measurement window, exclusions, support, credits or penalties. Any four are correct.

quiz.q: An SLA states RTO 15 minutes and RPO 5 minutes. What do they limit?
quiz.a: RTO limits service restoration time to 15 minutes. RPO limits data loss to the last 5 minutes.

quiz.q: Actual downtime is 25 minutes. SLA is 99.9% and SLO is 99.95% for a 30-day month. Which is breached, and are credits due?
quiz.a: Allowed downtime: SLA 43.2 minutes, SLO 21.6 minutes. 25 > 21.6, so the SLO is breached. 25 ≤ 43.2, so the SLA is met. No credits are due; freeze risky releases.

quiz.q: What is an error budget and what action follows when it is spent?
quiz.a: Budget = window × (1 − SLO). It is the allowed failure. When spent, stop risky releases and invest in reliability work.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry site reliability engineering (SRE) teams use error budgets to decide when to release and when to stop. Multi-cloud contracts make composite SLA arithmetic and exclusion clauses harder. Observability tools now measure SLIs from logs, traces and real-user data, not only probes. Search for 'SRE error budget', 'composite SLA' and 'RTO RPO' to go deeper.
